title: Westminster Quarters Chime
body:
Specifications

The Westminster quarters, also called the Cambridge quarters, are played on four bells or rods tuned to E, D, C, and G, with a fifth permutation that lacks the G bell. The chime was written in 1793-1794 for St Mary the Great, Cambridge, and was later adopted by the clock tower at the Palace of Westminster, where Big Ben hangs. It is the most widely used quarter chime in grandfather clocks.

Mechanism

The chime uses five permutations of the four notes: (1) E, D, C, G; (2) C, E, D, G; (2b) C, D, E, C; (3) E, C, D, G; and (4) G, D, E, C. The first quarter plays (1) alone, the half hour plays (2) then (2b), the third quarter plays (3), (4), then (1), and the full hour plays (2), (2b), (3), then (4), followed by the hour strikes. Each permutation is played as three quarter notes and a dotted half note, which gives the chime its familiar shape.

Maintenance

Keep the chime rods clean and free of dust, and check the hammer alignment so each hammer strikes its rod squarely. A rod that sounds dull usually has a hammer striking off-centre or a loose mounting. Never bend a chime rod to tune it; rods are tuned by grinding, and a bent rod will break.

Build and restoration guidance

When setting a Westminster chime barrel, start from the first quarter position and check that the barrel plays (1) alone before it plays the longer sequences, because the whole hour is built from the same five permutations in order. A barrel one step out will play the right notes in the wrong quarter.

Tools

Chime rod gauges, hammer alignment tool, screwdrivers, and a tuning reference.

title: Whittington Chime
body:
Specifications

The Whittington chime is an eight-bell chime associated with St Mary-le-Bow in London and with the Dick Whittington story, in which the bells ring out 'Turn again, Whittington'. It needs eight rods or bells, twice as many as Westminster, and it is offered as a second or third chime option on triple-chime grandfather clocks.

Mechanism

The first quarter plays eight notes running down the scale from the highest rod to the lowest, and each later quarter adds another eight notes, so the half hour plays sixteen, the third quarter twenty-four, and the full hour thirty-two, followed by the hour strikes. The descending scale at the first quarter is the Whittington's signature, and the later quarters build on it rather than repeating it.

Maintenance

Keep all eight rods clean and check the hammers in order, because one dead hammer breaks the descending scale and is obvious at the first quarter. Check the chime selector so the movement is fully on Whittington before testing, since a half-selected chime plays a mixture of two tunes.

Build and restoration guidance

When setting a Whittington barrel, verify the first quarter first: eight notes descending from the shortest rod to the longest. If the first quarter is correct, the later quarters follow, because the barrel is pinned as a single sequence used twice per hour.

Tools

Chime rod gauges, hammer tool, screwdrivers, and a scale reference.

title: St Michael Chime
body:
Specifications

The St Michael chime is an eight-bell chime associated with St Michael's Church in Charleston, South Carolina, whose bells were first rung there in 1764, and it is a standard option on triple-chime grandfather clocks. Like Whittington, it needs eight rods or bells, and its tune is distinct from both Whittington and Westminster.

Mechanism

The first quarter plays eight notes, and each later quarter adds eight more, so the half hour plays sixteen, the third quarter twenty-four, and the full hour thirty-two, followed by the hour strikes. The tune's shape differs from Whittington's descending scale, and the chime barrel is pinned with its own sequence, so the two eight-bell chimes are not interchangeable even though they share the same rod count.

Maintenance

Keep the eight rods clean, check the hammers in order, and test the chime selector's full travel, because a selector that stops short of St Michael will mix it with the neighbouring chime. A St Michael clock that plays Whittington at one quarter has a selector fault, not a barrel fault.

Build and restoration guidance

When setting a St Michael barrel, check the first quarter's eight notes against the movement's chime chart before checking the longer quarters, and confirm the hour strike follows the full sequence. Record which chime the selector positions correspond to, because the order varies by maker.

Tools

Chime rod gauges, hammer tool, screwdrivers, and the movement's chime chart.

title: Winchester Chime
body:
Specifications

The Winchester chime is a triple-chime option on many grandfather clocks, offered alongside Westminster and Whittington, and it is played on the same multi-rod chime set as the other two options. Its tune is distinct from both, and it is selected by the chime selector lever on the dial or the side of the movement.

Mechanism

The Winchester sequence accumulates through the hour like the other quarter chimes: a short sequence at the first quarter, a longer one at the half hour, longer still at the third quarter, and the full sequence at the hour, followed by the hour strikes. The chime barrel carries the Winchester tune on its own track, and the selector moves the hammers or the barrel to that track. Because makers pin Winchester differently, the record describes its structure and selection rather than asserting one maker's note string as universal.

Maintenance

Keep the rods clean, check the selector's full travel, and test all three chime options after any service, because a selector adjusted for one chime can drift off another. A Winchester clock that plays the wrong tune at one quarter usually has a selector or barrel-position fault.

Build and restoration guidance

When setting a triple-chime barrel, mark the Winchester track before removing the barrel, and verify the first quarter before the longer quarters. Never force the selector lever, because the selector fork bends easily and then no chime selects cleanly.

Tools

Chime rod gauges, selector adjustment tool, screwdrivers, and the movement's chime chart.

title: Big Ben Full Hour Sequence
body:
Specifications

The Big Ben full hour sequence is the Westminster quarters played in full at the top of the hour, followed by the hour strikes on the great bell, as heard from the clock tower at the Palace of Westminster. In a grandfather clock the same sequence is played on four chime rods, with the hour strike on a separate rod or on the lowest rod.

Mechanism

At the hour, the clock plays the full Westminster sequence, (2), (2b), (3), and (4), which is sixteen notes, and then strikes the hour: one strike for one o'clock, two for two, and so on up to twelve. The hour strike train is separate from the chime train, and the two must be synchronised so the strike begins only after the last chime note. That synchronisation is done by the chime train's locking and the strike train's warning.

Maintenance

Keep the hour strike hammer and the chime hammers aligned, and check that the strike does not begin early, because an early strike over the last chime note sounds like a fault even when both trains are healthy. Test the full hour at least once after any service, not just the quarters.

Build and restoration guidance

When synchronising, set the chime train to finish its full sequence before the strike train's warning releases, and count the hour strikes at three different hours, because a strike fault that shows at twelve may not show at three. Adjust the rack or count wheel, never the hands, to correct a wrong strike count.

Tools

Hammer alignment tool, screwdrivers, and a counting reference.

title: Passing Strike
body:
Specifications

A passing strike is a strike that sounds as the hands pass the hour, without a full striking train of its own, and it is used on clocks that need an hour sound but not a full striking movement. The strike is usually a single blow, or a small number of blows, triggered by the going train itself.

Mechanism

As the minute hand passes twelve, a pin or cam on the going train trips a hammer, which strikes a bell or gong once. The clock does not count the hours, so a passing strike cannot tell the listener which hour it is, only that an hour has passed. That simplicity is its advantage: there is no strike train to synchronise and no rack or count wheel to wear.

Maintenance

Keep the tripping pin clean and the hammer pivot oiled, and check that the strike sounds exactly at the hour, not before or after. A passing strike that sounds late usually has a bent tripping pin or a loose hammer, not a going-train fault.

Build and restoration guidance

When fitting a passing strike, set the tripping pin so the hammer falls exactly as the minute hand reaches twelve, and test at several hours, because a pin set for one hour may drift if the going train has shake. Do not add a counting mechanism to a passing strike; that converts it to a full strike and needs a separate train.

Tools

Small files, hammer pivot oil, screwdrivers, and a timing reference.

title: Full Hour Strike
body:
Specifications

A full hour strike counts the hours and strikes the correct number of blows for each hour, from one at one o'clock to twelve at twelve o'clock, using a dedicated striking train. It is the standard striking system on longcase clocks and is driven by its own weight or spring, separate from the going train.

Mechanism

Before the hour, the striking train is warned: a lever lifts and the train runs a short way until it is caught, ready to strike. At the hour the warning is released, the train runs, and the rack or count wheel lets it strike exactly the right number of blows, then locks it again. The warning step is what lets the strike begin promptly at the hour rather than lagging behind it.

Maintenance

Keep the strike train pivots oiled and the warning lever clean, and check the strike count at every hour after a service, because a strike that counts correctly at three may fail at twelve. A strike that runs on past the hour usually has a worn locking face, not a weak spring.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring a full strike, set the warning so the train is caught firmly, set the locking so it stops cleanly after the last blow, and test all twelve hours in order. Never adjust the hands to correct a wrong count; correct the rack or count wheel.

Tools

Strike train oil, warning lever gauge, screwdrivers, and a counting chart.

title: Count-Wheel Striking
body:
Specifications

Count-wheel striking, also called locking-plate striking, is the older striking system, in which a wheel with notches of increasing depth controls how many blows the strike train makes. It was used on early longcase and lantern clocks before the rack and snail became standard.

Mechanism

The count wheel turns a little at each strike, and its notches let the locking lever drop in after the correct number of blows. Because the wheel must complete a full cycle of 78 blows, the sum of one through twelve, before it repeats, the count wheel and the hands must stay in step. If they fall out of step, the clock strikes the wrong hour until the wheel is turned back into agreement, which is why count-wheel clocks have a strike-correction procedure.

Maintenance

Keep the count-wheel notches clean and the locking lever pivot oiled, and check the wheel's position after any hand adjustment. A count-wheel clock that strikes one hour out after the hands were moved has simply fallen out of step, and the correction is to let it strike until it agrees again, not to bend the lever.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, check every notch for wear, because a worn notch lets the train run one blow too many, and set the locking lever so it drops squarely into the notches. Test the full 78-blow cycle, not just one hour, before closing the movement.

Tools

Count-wheel gauge, locking lever tool, clock oil, and a 78-blow chart.

title: Rack-and-Snail Striking
body:
Specifications

Rack-and-snail striking is the later and now standard striking system, in which a snail cam on the hour wheel sets how far a rack can fall, and the rack's teeth set how many blows the strike train makes. It replaced the count wheel because it always strikes the hour the hands show, even after the hands are moved.

Mechanism

As the hour approaches, the rack is lifted and the snail turns with the hour wheel. At the hour the rack falls onto the snail's step for that hour, and the strike train runs, gathering up the rack one tooth per blow, until the rack is fully gathered and the train locks. Because the snail is driven by the hands, moving the hands forward automatically resets the strike count, so the clock cannot strike out of step the way a count-wheel clock can.

Maintenance

Keep the rack teeth and the snail steps clean, oil the rack pivot lightly, and check that the rack falls fully onto the snail at every hour. A rack that hangs up strikes too few blows, and the cause is usually dirt on the snail or a bent rack tooth, not the strike train.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, check the snail steps for wear, because a worn step makes one hour strike short, and set the gathering pallet so it takes one tooth per blow, no more and no less. Test all twelve hours after any rack work.

Tools

Rack gauge, snail step gauge, clock oil, and a counting chart.

title: Quarter-Hour Striking Train
body:
Specifications

The quarter-hour striking train is the separate train that plays the quarter chimes, distinct from the hour strike train and from the going train. On a triple-chime clock it also carries the chime barrel and the selector, and it is driven by its own weight or spring so the chimes do not drain the going train.

Mechanism

The going train trips the quarter train at each quarter, the train runs through its warning and then plays the barrel sequence for that quarter, and it locks again until the next quarter. The barrel turns once per hour on a Westminster movement, playing a longer part of its pinned sequence at each quarter, and the locking must be firm, or the train will overrun and play into the next quarter.

Maintenance

Keep the quarter train pivots oiled and the locking lever clean, and check that the train locks immediately after the last note of each quarter. A quarter train that plays on into the next quarter usually has a worn locking face or a weak locking spring.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, set the warning, the barrel position, and the locking as a set, because adjusting one without the others moves the fault rather than curing it. Test all four quarters in order, twice, before closing the movement.

Tools

Quarter train oil, locking lever tool, screwdrivers, and a quarter chart.

title: Ting-Tang Two-Bell Strike
body:
Specifications

The ting-tang strike uses two bells or gongs of different pitch, struck alternately, to mark the hour, and it is used on clocks where a single bell would be too plain but a full chime train is too large. The two notes alternate, high then low, for the full hour count.

Mechanism

At the hour the strike train drives two hammers alternately, one for the high bell and one for the low bell, so the listener hears ting-tang, ting-tang, for as many pairs as the hour requires, with a single extra blow on odd hours. The alternating action needs a strike train with two hammer levers timed to alternate, which is more complex than a single-bell strike but simpler than a chime barrel.

Maintenance

Keep both bells clean and both hammers aligned, because a hammer striking off-centre on one bell makes the alternation sound uneven. Check the hammer timing after any service, since one hammer running late breaks the ting-tang rhythm.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, set the two hammers to alternate evenly, check that each hammer lifts clear after its blow, and test at an odd hour and an even hour, because the odd hour's final single blow is where timing faults show.

Tools

Two-bell gauge, hammer alignment tool, clock oil, and screwdrivers.

title: Ave Maria Chime
body:
Specifications

The Ave Maria chime is a six-note chime option on some grandfather clocks, based on the melody of the Ave Maria, and it is offered where the owner wants a longer, more song-like quarter chime than Westminster's four notes. It is played on six rods or bells, and its tune is a short melody rather than a permutation of a few notes.

Mechanism

The chime plays a short melodic phrase at each quarter, accumulating through the hour like the other quarter chimes, so the half hour plays more of the melody than the first quarter, and the full hour plays the whole phrase followed by the hour strikes. Because the tune is melodic, its barrel is pinned as a melody, not as permutations, and the rods must be tuned to the melody's scale.

Maintenance

Keep the six rods clean and tuned, and check the hammers in melodic order, because one dead hammer breaks the melody in a way that a permutation chime hides. Test the full hour after any service, since the melody's end is where faults show.

Build and restoration guidance

When setting an Ave Maria barrel, verify the melody's first phrase before the longer quarters, and confirm the hour strike follows the full phrase. Record the rod tuning in the service notes, because a retuned rod changes the melody.

Tools

Chime rod gauges, hammer tool, screwdrivers, and a melody chart.

title: St Patrick Chime
body:
Specifications

The St Patrick chime is a chime option on some triple-chime and multi-chime grandfather clocks, named for St Patrick, and it is played on the same multi-rod set as the other chime options. It is less common than Westminster, Whittington, and St Michael, and makers pin it differently, so its description here covers its structure and selection.

Mechanism

The St Patrick sequence accumulates through the hour like the other quarter chimes, with a short sequence at the first quarter and the full sequence at the hour, followed by the hour strikes. The barrel carries the St Patrick tune on its own track, and the selector moves the hammers or barrel to that track. Because makers differ, the record does not assert one maker's note string as universal, and the movement's own chime chart is the authority for the exact notes.

Maintenance

Keep the rods clean, check the selector's full travel, and test all chime options after any service, because a selector adjusted for one chime can drift off another. A St Patrick clock playing the wrong tune at one quarter usually has a selector or barrel-position fault.

Build and restoration guidance

When setting a multi-chime barrel, mark the St Patrick track before removing the barrel, verify the first quarter before the longer quarters, and never force the selector lever, because the selector fork bends easily.

Tools

Chime rod gauges, selector tool, screwdrivers, and the movement's chime chart.

title: Musical Chime Barrel
body:
Specifications

A musical chime barrel is a pinned cylinder that plays a full melody, rather than a quarter-chime permutation, when the clock strikes or when a lever is pulled. It is used on musical longcase clocks, which play a tune on the hour, and on clocks with a separate musical movement.

Mechanism

Pins on the barrel lift levers as the barrel turns, and each lever trips a hammer that strikes a rod or bell, so the melody is stored as pin positions on the barrel. The barrel is driven by its own spring or weight, governed so it turns at a steady speed, and the tune's tempo depends on the governor, not on the going train. Changing the tune means changing the barrel, which is why musical clocks often came with several interchangeable barrels.

Maintenance

Keep the barrel pins clean and straight, oil the barrel pivots lightly, and check the governor, because a slow governor makes the tune drag and a fast one makes it rush. A tune that plays correctly at the start but rushes at the end usually has a weakening governor spring.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring a musical barrel, check every pin for tightness, replace missing pins with new ones of the same height, and test the tune at full wind and low wind, because the governor must hold tempo at both. Never file a pin to change a note; move or replace it.

Tools

Barrel pin gauges, governor tool, clock oil, and a melody chart.

title: Strike Train Warning and Let-Off
body:
Specifications

Warning and let-off are the two steps that make a striking clock strike promptly at the hour. Warning prepares the strike train a few minutes before the hour, and let-off releases it exactly at the hour, so the first blow falls on the hour rather than after it.

Mechanism

A few minutes before the hour, the going train lifts the warning lever, the strike train runs a short way until its locking lever catches it, and the train waits, warned. At the hour the going train trips the let-off, the locking lever releases, and the train runs through its full strike. If warning fails, the strike lags; if let-off fails, the strike does not sound at all, or sounds at the wrong time.

Maintenance

Keep the warning and let-off levers clean and their pivots oiled, and check the warning a few minutes before the hour, not just the strike at the hour. A strike that lags usually has a warning lever that lifts late or a let-off that sticks.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring, set the warning to engage firmly a few minutes before the hour, set the let-off to release cleanly at the hour, and test the warning at every hour, because a warning that works at three may fail at twelve if the cam is worn.

Tools

Warning lever gauge, let-off tool, clock oil, and screwdrivers.

title: Grand Sonnerie
body:
Specifications

Grand sonnerie is the striking mode in which the clock chimes the quarters and then strikes the full hour count after every quarter, not only at the top of the hour. At the first quarter it plays the quarter chime and then strikes one, at the half hour it plays the half-hour chime and then strikes the hour count, and so on, so the listener always hears both the quarter and the hour.

Mechanism

Grand sonnerie needs both a quarter chime train and a full hour strike train, and the two must be sequenced so the chime finishes before the strike begins. The strike train is therefore triggered by the chime train's completion, not directly by the going train, and the whole sequence takes longer than a simple quarter chime. Petite sonnerie, by contrast, strikes the hour only at the top of the hour and plays the quarters alone at the other quarters.

Maintenance

Keep both trains oiled and synchronised, and check the sequence at every quarter after a service, because a grand sonnerie clock that strikes before the chime finishes has a sequencing fault, not a chime fault. Test at the first quarter as well as the hour, since the first quarter is where the hour strike after a quarter is most likely to be missed.

Build and restoration guidance

When restoring grand sonnerie, set the chime train to complete and lock before the strike train is released, and test all four quarters in order, counting both the chime notes and the hour strikes at each. Never shorten the sequence to cure a fault; find the sequencing lever that is out of adjustment.
